CHALLENGE C0087 | Sorting by `timestamp_utc` violates distributed systems principles (Hard Constraint 3: Wall clocks are for human display only, subject to NTP skew and non-monotonicity). In an append-only hash chain, the sequence index provides the only true, globally consistent causal ordering. Modifying `trace_finding()` to sort by wall-clock timestamps would reorder causally sequential events on clock skew, explicitly breaking causal consistency. The code correctly sorts by `indices` and MUST NOT be changed to use timestamps.

CHALLENGE C0106 | The proposed fix is insufficient to prevent evidence tampering. Comparing `record["chain_hash"] == proof["chain_hash"]` only checks the dictionary fields, leaving the `sealed_body` completely unverified. An attacker can falsify the `payload` inside `sealed_body` while leaving `chain_hash` unchanged, and `verify_bundle()` will incorrectly report the bundle as valid. The `sealed_body` MUST be cryptographically re-hashed to prove integrity (see F001).

DESCRIPTION: FIND: In `bench/evidence.py`, `EvidenceStore.verify_bundle()` fails to verify the cryptographic integrity of the bundled records. It only validates that the inclusion proofs are mathematically correct for a given `chain_hash`. It never recomputes the hash of the `sealed_body` to ensure it actually matches the `chain_hash`.
FOLLOW: Downstream auditors relying on `verify_bundle()` to authenticate evidence bundles will accept tampered payloads as cryptographically proven. An attacker can alter any field in `record["sealed_body"]` (like `payload` or `artifact_type`), leave `chain_hash` unchanged, and the bundle will verify perfectly.
ANALYSE: CONFIRMED. The code iterates over `zip(bundle.records, bundle.inclusion_proofs)` and directly calls `self._chain.verify_inclusion_proof(proof, bundle.merkle_root)`. The record's content is completely unverified. Even if C0106 is applied, it only compares dictionary string values without cryptographically hashing the body.

DESCRIPTION: FIND: In `bench/evidence.py`, `_classify_event` incorrectly classifies merge events for the source finding. The protocol format for merges is `MERGE target_id <- source_id` (e.g., `MERGE C0002 <- C0001`). The function checks `f"MERGE {finding_id}" in payload_str`. This successfully matches the target finding (`C0002`), but fails for the source finding (`C0001`) because the string contains `"<- C0001"`, not `"MERGE C0001"`.
FOLLOW: When tracing provenance for a finding that was merged into another, the merge event will be incorrectly classified as "submitted" instead of "merged", generating misleading provenance traces for the source finding (e.g. reporting "submitted by..." instead of "merge-linked by...").
ANALYSE: CONFIRMED. The substring `f"MERGE {finding_id}"` enforces that the finding ID immediately follows the word "MERGE". This logically misses the right-hand side of the merge syntax. Adding a check for the merge source operator `<- {finding_id}` correctly resolves this.
